secret.title: The Secret Number
secret.intro: Each duelist locks in an undisclosed 4-digit code. Every code must adhere to strict mathematical validity constraints:
secret.footer: 4 unique digits kept strictly hidden inside an encrypted vault.

guess.title: The Guess Protocol
guess.intro: Every round, transmit 4 non-repeating digits. You receive instantaneous positional telemetry.
guess.footer: Repeat guesses are prohibited by UI. Every probe burns one turn token.

firstMove.title: Who Moves First?
firstMove.body: System flips an algorithmic 50/50 token. First mover gets initiative; second mover gets retrospective balance.

matrix.title: The Deduction Matrix
matrix.intro: Clues are calculated in real-time after every submitted attempt. Memorize these three tactical signatures:

pico.description: Correct digit locked in the exact right position.

pala.description: Digit exists inside the vault, but is currently in the wrong slot.

miss.label: MISS
miss.description: Digit is totally absent from the secret number. Completely eliminated.

example.title: A Turn, Dissected

step.one: Right digit & right slot. Target anchored.
step.two: 1 exists in vault (Slot 3), but transmitted into Slot 2.
step.three: 5 is completely unassigned in 3719. Discard it.
step.four: Identical position and value lock. Second Pico.

example.note: Note: The clue does NOT specify which digit caused which signal!

directive.title: Master Deduction Directive
directive.body: If your initial guess yields <yellow>1 Pico</yellow> and <pink>2 Palas</pink>, you already possess 3 out of 4 correct vault numbers (75% precision). <white>Never randomize on Turn 2.</white> Keep 3 numbers, permute positions, and swap only the single suspect candidate.

sudden.title: The 12-Turn Sudden Death Protocol
sudden.body: If neither duelist decrypts all 4 digits within 12 attempts, the duel terminates in a <white>Tactical Draw</white>. Both secret vaults are unveiled simultaneously for mutual review.

strategy.title: Advanced strategy
strategy.subtitle: How to win more duels: read every clue, shrink the candidate list and never waste a turn.

stats.label: candidates left at most after your first guess

strategy.statsNote: The average comes from a simulation of 300 random codes always playing a possible code: 5 guesses on average and 8 in the worst case observed.

items.title: Your first guess: any 4 distinct digits
items.body: The nine digits are interchangeable, so every opening is equivalent: they split the 3,024 codes the same way and leave 840 at worst. Use 1234 and focus on reading the clue.

items.title: Picos + Palas = how many digits you got right
items.body: The sum tells you how many digits of your guess are in the secret, regardless of position. First find out which 4 digits they are; then where they go.

items.title: Don't forget to count the digit you haven't tried
items.body: If two guesses cover 8 digits (for example 1234 and 5678) and together they add up to 3 hits, the 9 is in the code. If they add up to 4, the 9 is not.

items.title: Always play a code that could still be the secret
items.body: Before sending, check that your guess would have produced the same clues you already received. That way no turn is wasted and every attempt could be the winning one. The board's "possible" counter shows how many candidates remain.

items.title: Zero hits is the best news
items.body: A guess with no Picos and no Palas eliminates four digits at once: out of 3,024 codes only 120 remain.

items.title: Change a single slot to isolate a digit
items.body: If you repeat a guess changing just one digit, the difference between the two clues tells you what happened to that digit: whether it came in, went out or only changed type.

items.title: When Picos + Palas is 4, only the order is left
items.body: You already have all four digits and there are at most 24 arrangements. Lock in with the Picos and try only the permutations that respect every previous clue.

items.title: Hide your secret without patterns
items.body: Avoid sequences (1234, 9876), dates and easy-to-guess numbers. The "Random" button when setting your code is the best option. In Grandmaster you have 60 s per turn: if time runs out, the system sends a random guess for you, so plan while the bot thinks.

example.title: A match solved in 5 guesses
example.intro: Secret code: 7314 (the opponent can't see it). Every guess is a code that could still have been the secret.
turns: Opening: 3 of these 4 digits are in the code, but only one is in its slot. Of 3,024 codes, 180 remain.
Still a possible code given the first clue: it keeps three digits and tests the 5. The total drops to 2 hits and 32 remain.
It tests the 6 and reorders the rest. Two Palas and no Pico leave only 9 candidates.
With 9 candidates you pick one that separates them well. This clue leaves a single possible code.
Only one was left: 4 Picos and victory on guess 5, with 7 guesses to spare.
example.outro: The key wasn't guessing: it was eliminating. Every clue shrinks the candidates and the next guess comes from the ones that survive.

mistakes.title: Mistakes that cost matches
items: Reusing digits you already know are not in the secret.
Ignoring Palas: a Pala means the digit is there, just in another slot.
Changing many digits at once: you won't know what caused each change in the clue.
Guessing at random when few candidates remain instead of checking which ones fit every clue.
Spending "test" guesses that can no longer be the secret.

cta.title: Take it to the arena
cta.body: Practice turns these principles into reflexes. Start against the AI on Novice and level up.
